hints: Look first at what type of reaction each equation shows, acid-base or redox, by checking oxidation numbers.
In equation 2 sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is reduced to $\text{SO}_2$ while $\text{Q}^-$ is oxidised to $\text{Q}_2$, so ask which halides are strong enough reducing agents to do this.
Remember the trend with concentrated sulfuric acid, chloride gives only $\text{HCl}$, bromide gives $\text{SO}_2$, and iodide gives $\text{SO}_2$ plus further reduction, then match both equations.
walkthrough:
**Understand equation 1**

All halide ions do this reaction. It is simply an acid-base proton transfer.

$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Q}^- \rightarrow \text{HSO}_4^- + \text{HQ}$$
This gives $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ or $\text{HI}$. So equation 1 does not identify Q.

**Understand equation 2**

This is a redox reaction. Check the oxidation numbers.

$$\text{S in H}_2\text{SO}_4 (+6) \rightarrow \text{S in SO}_2 (+4)$$
Sulfur is reduced, so $\text{Q}^-$ must be oxidised to $\text{Q}_2$. Only a strong enough reducing agent can do this.

**Apply the halide trend with concentrated sulfuric acid**

$\text{Cl}^-$ is not a strong enough reducing agent, so it stops at equation 1 and no $\text{SO}_2$ forms.

$\text{Br}^-$ reduces $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$ and is itself oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$. $\text{I}^-$ is even stronger and also reduces $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$ (as well as to S and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in further reactions). So Q that gives both equations must be bromide or iodide.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ only undergoes equation 1 to give $\text{HCl}$. It cannot reduce concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$, so it cannot give equation 2. $\text{Br}^-$ can, but $\text{Cl}^-$ cannot.
options.B: Correct. Both $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ undergo equation 1 to form $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$, and both are strong enough reducing agents to carry out equation 2, reducing S(+6) to S(+4) in $\text{SO}_2$ while being oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$ or $\text{I}_2$.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ only gives white fumes of $\text{HCl}$ with concentrated sulfuric acid. No reduction to $\text{SO}_2$ occurs, so equation 2 would never be observed.
options.D: Incorrect because it is too narrow. $\text{I}^-$ certainly gives equation 2, but $\text{Br}^-$ also gives $\text{SO}_2$ by the same equation. Students choosing this often remember iodide as the strongest reductant but forget bromide also reduces to $\text{SO}_2$.
